screens.eyebrow: A practice plan for my clients · Trauma
screens.title: Four Weeks of Steady Ground
screens.sub: Deepening what you started, in small doses, inside your window
screens.byline: Set-up takes about 15 minutes. After that, five to ten minutes on most days.

screens.title: How the plan works

blocks.p: On most days. That is the dose. Going slower is always allowed.
Rate how you feel from 0 (calm) to 10 (very distressed). Stay at about a 3 or below. Above a 4, stop and orient. That is the rule, not a failure.

blocks.h: We do not go into what happened
blocks.p: Everything here is about now. If memories come up, you do not have to follow them. Orient, then tell me in session.
Use the section name at the top to jump to your week. Each week takes about four minutes to read and set up.

screens.note: Finished Steady Ground first? Good, this builds on it. If not, start there. Not for everyone: if it ever feels like too much, tell me and we will change it.

screens.text: Regulation is not staying calm. It is getting back.
screens.sub: Everyone floods sometimes, loud or quiet. Repair is the skill.

cards.p: Tell your body where and when it is, every day.
Find something steady and let your body get to know it.
Practice coming back, and being kind to the part that left.
Decide what stays, in the smallest version that still works.

screens.title: How the four weeks fit together
screens.summary: A walk through the plan, the 3-or-below rule, and when to stop and tell me.
bullets: How to check your distress level

screens.title: Week 1: Orient

cards.p: Orienting, one to two minutes, same time most days. It comes before any breath work.
A ten-second check-in: revved up, in your window, or powered down? Just notice.
Pick one early signal: the first body sign that your alarm is going off.

screens.intro: This week you are collecting information, not fixing anything.

screens.title: Here, now, this room
steps: Let your head and eyes turn slowly. Take in the room one piece at a time.
Find something in a color you like. Rest your eyes there.
Notice one sound near you and one farther away.
Feel your feet and what is holding you. Say, "It is today. I am here."

guide.text: Let your eyes move slowly around the room. No hurry.
Find something you like the look of. Let your eyes rest on it.
Notice one sound close to you and one sound farther away.
Feel your feet on the floor. Press them down a little.
Feel what is holding you up: the chair, the bed, the floor.
Say, out loud or in your head: "It is today. I am here."
Let your breath do whatever it wants. You do not have to manage it.

screens.guideEnd: Good. Notice if anything is even a little different.
cautions: If anything feels strange, look at something familiar and say today's date out loud.

screens.title: Week 1 tracker
screens.intro: Tick a box when you do it. Skipped days are just days.

screens.title: What did you notice this week?
screens.prompt: When did your alarm go off this week, and what helped you remember it was now?
screens.focus: Keep to the present and to what helped. Do not ask what the alarm was about.
screens.placeholder: For example: in the grocery store, my chest tightened and I looked at the shelves...

screens.title: Find something steady
steps: Think of something that feels steady, kind, or safe enough: a place, an object, a pet, a person, a color. Choose something simple, and avoid anything tied up with loss or mixed feelings.
Look at it, or hold it in mind, for about twenty seconds.
Notice your body. Anything softer, warmer, heavier, or easier? Even slightly?
If you notice nothing, or it stirs something hard, stop and orient. Try a different resource another day.
screens.lead: A resource is not a cure. It is a place for your body to rest a little.
cautions: Stay at about a 3 out of 10 or below.
Later, in session, we may practice moving attention gently between something steady and something a bit uncomfortable. That is not for doing alone yet.

screens.title: Week 2 tracker
screens.intro: Orienting stays on the list. It is your base.

screens.title: Return and repair: being kind to the part that left
screens.summary: How to come back to now, and how to be gentle with the part that protected you in the moment.
bullets: Kindness toward a part that did its job

screens.title: Return, then repair
steps: Notice: "I have left my window." Name it: "A part of me is revved up," or "powered down."
Orient first. Then the cooling breath if you are revved up and it suits you. Notice what is even slightly different.
When you are settled, say what happened plainly, with no verdict: "I went quiet in the meeting."
Thank the part: "You were trying to protect me." Ask what it needed. Listen for a word or a feeling, not a story.
Offer it one small thing, such as a hand on your chest or a glass of water.
screens.lead: Keep the parts language light. Names like the Guard or the Tender One are optional.
screens.eyebrow: For after you froze, snapped, or went quiet
screens.note: Repair is not about being perfect. It is about not leaving yourself alone in it.

screens.title: A return or a repair
screens.prompt: Think of a time this week you left your window and came back, even partway. What helped? What did the part that left seem to need?
screens.focus: Stay in this week and in the present. Do not ask what the part is reacting to from the past.
screens.placeholder: For example: the Guard went on high alert at the noise, then I looked around...

screens.title: Week 4: Rhythm

cards.p: What is the bad-day version? One look around the room counts.
Anything that feels like another thing to perform. Drop it, and tell me.

screens.intro: You will probably not keep doing everything forever. Good. Let's find the smallest version that still works.

screens.title: My rhythm
screens.prompt: What do you want to keep, shrink, or drop? What is your tiny version for a hard day?
screens.placeholder: For example: keep orienting each morning, drop the evening check-in...

screens.title: What to bring to session
screens.text: Four weeks of steadiness, built in small doses.
items: What do we want to keep, shrink, or drop?
Which parts were most active, and what did they seem to need?
Where did coming back happen, even a little?
